---
title: "Discussion"
---

::: {.rev}
We studied blood DNA methylation in 2,491 older adults with dementia follow-up for up to 13.4 years, whose cognition was assessed at baseline and again about five years later. Participants fell into six groups by clinical course: stable normal, normal-to-MCI (normal cognition followed by mild cognitive impairment, MCI), stable MCI, normal-to-dementia, MCI-to-dementia, and prevalent dementia (dementia at baseline). We asked whether methylation differed among these groups and whether the differences followed their clinical course. At 403 methylation (CpG) sites, at least one group differed significantly from the stable normal group; we summarized these sites with two data-reduction methods, a variational autoencoder (VAE) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP). Two findings emerged: the methylation summaries formed a gradient that broadly followed clinical course, and participants with MCI did not share a common methylation profile.
:::

### [A methylation gradient]{.rev}

::: {.rev}
Both VAE and UMAP condensed the 403 sites into six summary dimensions, and in both methods the groups fell along a gradient that broadly followed clinical course: from those who stayed free of dementia, through those who developed it during follow-up, to those who already had it at baseline. The methylation differences of established dementia were thus already partly present, at the group level, years before diagnosis in participants who later developed dementia. The two methods rest on different mathematical principles yet captured the same gradient, which argues against an artifact of either method, and the gradient persisted when more weakly associated sites were added.
:::

::: {.rev}
*APOE* genotype, which was not used to build the dimensions, also differed along several of them (@fig-apoe-boxplots), with higher-risk genotypes shifted toward the dementia end of the gradient. Genotype-related and progression-related methylation variation therefore appear to coincide, consistent with reports linking *APOE* genotype to methylation differences [@RN92], but our data cannot show whether the genotype-related differences contribute to progression or merely accompany it.
:::

### MCI findings

::: {.rev}
MCI varies in which cognitive abilities are affected [@RN94], and only a fraction of people with MCI develop dementia [@RN95; @RN96]. Our two MCI groups that did not develop dementia — normal-to-MCI and stable MCI — differed in methylation from each other and from the groups that developed dementia.
:::

::: {.rev}
The stable MCI group had summary dimensions similar to those of the stable normal group. However, it was the only group with large differences at 60 of the 403 CpG sites, and these differences did not follow the dementia-associated pattern. They may explain why, in the VAE, the center of the stable MCI group lay well to one side of the path that ran from the stable normal group through the groups that developed dementia to prevalent dementia, so that the path detoured through it (Figure [-@fig-scatter-peak]E–F); the differences may reflect processes other than progression toward dementia.
:::

::: {.rev}
At the group level, methylation already differed by later course among participants who were cognitively normal at baseline: in those who went on to develop dementia, differences from the stable normal group followed the pattern of established dementia, whereas in those who developed only MCI (the normal-to-MCI group) they ran in the opposite direction (@fig-normal2mci). This held whether few or many sites were analyzed, and at both individual sites and summary dimensions, pointing to a coordinated feature of the methylome rather than a few loci [@RN86; @RN97]. MCI may therefore include biologically distinct courses, only some leading toward dementia, which could help explain its variable presentation.
:::

### Stage-specific biology

The earliest transition, [normal-to-MCI]{.rev}, was [the only group]{.rev} enriched for several functional categories — ion transport and regulation, synaptic function and organization, and extracellular matrix organization — that together [point to]{.rev} cellular communication and structural integrity. These processes align with established evidence of synaptic disruption and extracellular matrix remodeling in early cognitive decline [@RN49; @RN55; @RN56]. Immune response terms were likewise concentrated in this early transition rather than in advancing disease. The [stable MCI]{.rev} group carried hypoxic responses, which promote pathological protein accumulation and memory deficits [@RN50; @RN52]. [The MCI-to-dementia group]{.rev} was enriched for hormone signaling and for cell migration and organization [@RN57; @RN58; @RN59]. In prevalent dementia, cell-cycle regulation was the only [category specific to this group]{.rev}, consistent with aberrant cell cycle re-entry in late-stage neurodegeneration [@RN53; @RN54].

At the two ends of the progression, the [numbers of significant CpG sites and of enriched biological processes]{.rev} ran in opposite directions: prevalent dementia carried most of the 403 significant sites (326) but yielded only 22 enriched biological processes, whereas [the normal-to-MCI group]{.rev} reached genome-wide significance at just five sites yet yielded [152]{.rev} processes, [137]{.rev} of them [significant only in this group]{.rev}. Because the enrichment analysis drew a fixed number of top-ranked CpG sites from every group, the gene sets were of comparable size. [The number of enriched terms is nonetheless not a measure of biological activity; addressing that directly would require further studies in brain tissue.]{.rev}

### Limitations

Clinical staging carries a degree of uncertainty, particularly at the intermediate MCI stage. Diagnoses followed a standardized, adjudicated protocol supported by the fully digitized Icelandic health care records (see Methods) [@RN1; @RN63], and we counted only study-based diagnoses of MCI. Because cognition was assessed only at the two study examinations, some participants [in the normal-to-dementia group]{.rev} may have passed through an unrecorded MCI stage; direct progression from normal cognition to dementia is nonetheless well documented, accounting for close to 40% of converters even in cohorts with annual assessment [@RN87]. [Participants classified as dementia-free may have died before developing dementia or developed it after surveillance ended; excluding those followed for under 5 years left most effect sizes at the 403 sites largely unchanged, but some CpG sites may reflect survival rather than dementia risk.]{.rev}

Blood methylation is an indirect surrogate for central nervous system biology[. Some]{.rev} transition groups were relatively small, so several group-specific estimates were likely underpowered and require replication in larger cohorts.

::: {.rev}
The three groups cognitively normal at baseline already differed in cognitive scores (@tbl-baseline), as expected before diagnosis [@RN102; @RN35], although most scores lay within the stable normal group's range. Adjusting for these scores preserved the direction and most of the size of every genome-wide significant association, and all prevalent dementia associations remained nominally significant; because cognitive decline is part of what defines dementia, such adjustment also removes disease-related signal. The study used one Icelandic cohort with methylation analyzed at baseline only, so trajectories were inferred across groups rather than within individuals, and prediction of individual course was not tested.
:::

The pathway analyses relied on rank-based CpG selection to keep the gene sets comparable across groups, which prioritizes relative rather than absolute significance (see Methods). Because selection was relative, the top-ranked lists for the four transition groups consisted almost entirely of sub-threshold sites, so the processes enriched in those groups are suggestive[, partly overlap through related terms, and need confirmation in brain tissue]{.rev}. Comparisons were made relative to the stable normal or prevalent dementia group, so the results may not generalize to studies whose design, source population, or mix of dementia groups differs. The associations reported here are observational and do not establish causality.

::: {.rev}
Together, these findings indicate that blood DNA methylation differs years before dementia is diagnosed, and that the processes enriched at the early and late transitions differ. Their main contribution is biological. First, MCI was not a single methylation state: the normal-to-MCI, stable MCI and MCI-to-dementia groups each differed from the stable normal group in a different way, consistent with MCI as a heterogeneous clinical state whose courses methylation may help distinguish. Second, the CpG sites and processes identified here are candidates for mechanistic work: whether these methylation differences alter the expression of nearby genes, and how non-genetic factors modify them, can be tested with expression data and repeated measures. Methylation patterns that change along the clinical course may also point to processes worth examining as treatment targets, once replicated in independent cohorts.
:::
